question: When a machine takes over the tasks a job is named for, what happens to the people who do that job, and especially to the newest workers who used to learn on those tasks?

issues.note: Hard cut from the stylised 3D desk to a sepia archival photo of real people at a wind tunnel. The look of the world changes completely with no transition.
Narration mentions the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and spacecraft, but the picture is the same generic Langley desk. Nothing on screen shows JPL, so the picture does not match the narration.
Dark, near-unreadable ladder shot (symbolic, never explained) cuts abruptly to the bright dusk street. The ladder image has no clear link to the narration.
The 'second kind of work' corridor of dark cabinets is abstract. The jump from the lit classroom to a black corridor is hard to read at first.
Quote card stays on screen for about 12 s (R11.1 to R11.3), with only text and no new visual.
The same dark office stays on screen for about 16 s (R14.5 to R14.8) with only small changes. It reads as repeated footage.
The same dark, empty office again for about 16 s (R15.5 to R15.8). The view barely changes.
The dark office persists for another 16 s (R16.1 to R16.4). Together with R14.5 and R15.5 this is a long stretch of near-identical imagery, at the film's most abstract and most important argument.
The programmer-at-desk scene stays static for about 16 s (R10.3 to R10.6) while the quote is read.
